record.paper_title: Open questions on defining and computing the vapour-liquid surface tension by virial and test transformation approaches
record.context_brief: relation of computed tensions to Laplace thermodynamics
record.original_question: How can surface-tension values produced by virial, test-area, test-transformation, or other derivative-based microscopic methods for spherical vapour-liquid interfaces be related to the thermodynamic target value at the Laplace dividing surface, where the absolute and total-differential surface tensions coincide as σ_L = γ_L? If a method instead computes a surface tension associated with another dividing-surface notion ν, radius R_ν, or micromechanical construction, what closure relation or formalism can connect R_ν and γ_ν to the Laplace radius R_L and Laplace surface tension γ_L so that the computed quantity is not thermodynamically useless?

evidence.quote: This work addresses four problems in defining and computing the surface tension of vapour-liquid interfaces: (1) The apparent kinetic contribution to the surface tension, and what it is that makes it appear; (2) the problem of defining the local virial, which for some purposes appears to be necessary; (3) the disagreement between results for spherical interfaces when using different methods, specifically the virial and the test area method; (4) how the surface tension values obtained from these methods can be related to the definition of the surface tension from thermodynamics – since if they cannot, it is a meaningless exercise to compute them. At the end, all these problems remain unsolved: They are “open questions.”

there can be no doubt what quantity we must be interested in obtaining: The surface tension for the Laplace dividing surface, where the absolute and total-differential definitions of the surface tension become equivalent,σL = γL. This is commonly understood, but it deserves pointing out that the above analysis only confirms it. Any method that computes a surface tension other than this must either permit relating it toγL, so that it can be determined indirectly, or it is from the standpoint of interfacialthermodynamics completely useless and can only play a role within a different formalism that can make proper use of the respectivemicromechanics.
So it is in fact possible to obtainγν as a free energy derivative for someν, just not forν = L. Together with some closure relation, it might be possible to connectRν to RL, and γν to γL.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider a spherical vapour–liquid interface in equilibrium. In the Gibbsian thermodynamics of curved interfaces, every choice of a dividing surface of radius R assigns a surface tension; two natural definitions are the absolute surface tension σ(R) (defined from the grand-potential excess per unit area at the chosen dividing surface) and the total-differential surface tension γ(R) (defined as the appropriate free-energy derivative with respect to interfacial area at fixed thermodynamic constraints). There is a unique Laplace dividing surface, of radius R_L, on which these two definitions coincide:
   σ_L := σ(R_L) = γ(R_L) =: γ_L,
and γ_L is the thermodynamically meaningful surface tension entering the Laplace equation Δp = 2γ_L / R_L.

Microscopic (e.g. molecular-simulation) methods for spherical interfaces — such as the mechanical/virial route based on a chosen local stress tensor, the test-area method, more general test-transformation methods, and other derivative-based approaches — typically produce a surface tension γ_ν associated with some dividing-surface notion ν of radius R_ν (or with a particular micromechanical construction), where in general ν ≠ L.

Problem. (a) Determine, for each such microscopic method (virial with a specified contour for the local stress, test-area, test-transformation, and analogous derivative-based methods), the dividing-surface notion ν and radius R_ν that the method effectively realises for a spherical vapour–liquid interface, and characterise the corresponding surface tension γ_ν as a free-energy derivative.
(b) Derive an explicit closure relation linking (R_ν, γ_ν) to (R_L, γ_L), so that γ_L can be recovered from the microscopically computed γ_ν together with auxiliary equilibrium data (e.g. the bulk pressures, density profile, or other thermodynamic functions of the interface).
(c) If no such closure exists for a given method, prove that γ_ν cannot be related to γ_L within interfacial thermodynamics, and identify the alternative formalism (if any) within which γ_ν has operational meaning.
artifact.status_search_result: The originating discussion explicitly frames this as one of four "open questions" that remain unsolved, including how microscopically computed surface tensions for curved interfaces can be related to the Laplace surface tension γ_L. No subsequent work establishing a general closure relation between (R_ν, γ_ν) and (R_L, γ_L) for arbitrary derivative-based microscopic methods was located.

status_evidence.snippet: At the end, all these problems remain unsolved: They are 'open questions.'
